H1.text: Wet clay hits a wall, and sticks. Two railway coaches couple up, and roll away as one.

H2.text: In each crash, the bodies join. And something seems to vanish.

H3.text: In the college lab, Aarav rolls a trolley into a still one. Sticky pads on the front. They lock together.

H4.text: Same mass, so the pair rolls at half the speed. Momentum is fine. But half the kinetic energy is gone. Where did it go?

H5.text: Let's find out, and measure exactly how much.

P1.text: When two bodies stick together after a hit, and move as one, it is called a perfectly inelastic collision.

P2.text: Momentum is still kept. The pushes between them are internal.

P3.text: But kinetic energy is not kept. Some of it turns into heat, sound and bent pads.

S1.text: Our motion notebook. Trolley A, one kilogram, rolls at six metres per second. Trolley B, two kilograms, waits at rest.

S2.text: They hit, and lock. Now one body of three kilograms rolls at two metres per second.

S3.text: Momentum: six before. Three times two, six after. Kept.

S4.text: Kinetic energy: eighteen joules before. Only six after. Twelve joules lost. On the graph, the total drops, and never comes back.

S5.text: Slow-mo replay. Freeze in the middle of the crunch.

S6.text: The pads are squashed. The pushes are equal and opposite, so momentum moves from A to B.

S7.text: But the pads do not spring back. That stored energy never returns. It warms the pads, and makes the bang.

S8.text: Now swap them. Two kilograms rolls at six into the one kilogram trolley. Will more energy be lost, or less? Pause and decide.

S9.text: Less! They roll on at four. Thirty six joules before, twenty four after. Only twelve lost, one third.

S10.text: So the loss depends on which one moves.

D1.text: Now the formulas, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. Momentum before equals momentum after. m one u one plus m two u two equals m one plus m two, times v.

D3.text: Step two. So the common velocity v is the total momentum divided by the total mass.

D4.text: Step three. Kinetic energy lost is the energy before minus the energy after.

D5.text: Step four. Put v in and simplify. The loss is half, times m one m two over m one plus m two, times u one minus u two, squared.

D6.text: Check run one. Half, times two thirds, times thirty six. Twelve joules.

T1.text: Remember this. When bodies stick together, momentum is kept, but kinetic energy is lost.

R1.text: But why must energy be lost? Link by link.

R2.text: Kinetic energy can be written as p squared over two m.

R3.text: In the crash, the momentum p stays the same.

R4.text: But after sticking, that same p is carried by a bigger mass.

R5.text: Same p on top, bigger m below. So the kinetic energy must get smaller.

K1.text: Side by side. Two kilograms each. One at six metres per second, one at rest.

K2.text: Elastic: they swap. Zero and six. All thirty six joules kept.

K3.text: Perfectly inelastic: they stick, and roll at three. Eighteen joules kept, eighteen lost. That is the biggest loss a collision can have.

K4.text: Now you try. Two equal trolleys at the same speed hit head on, and stick. What fraction of the kinetic energy is lost? Pause and decide.

K5.text: All of it! Their momenta are equal and opposite, so the total is zero. The pair stops dead.

W2.text: Fifty grams of putty at twenty metres per second hits a nine hundred and fifty gram trolley at rest, and sticks. Find the speed and the energy lost.

W3.text: Momentum before: zero point zero five times twenty. One kilogram metre per second.

W4.text: The total mass is one kilogram. So v is one metre per second.

W5.text: Energy before: half, times zero point zero five, times twenty squared. Ten joules. After: half a joule.

W6.text: So nine point five joules are lost. Ninety five percent!

X2.text: Many students think perfectly inelastic means all the kinetic energy is lost.

X3.text: No. Only the share needed to make them move together is lost. In run one, six of the eighteen joules stayed.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In numericals on common velocity, energy lost, and bullets stuck in blocks.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A twenty gram bullet at five hundred metres per second sticks in a four point nine eight kilogram hanging block. g is ten. How high does the block swing? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Twenty centimetres.

A2.text: Momentum is kept in the hit. Zero point zero two times five hundred is ten.

A3.text: The total mass is five kilograms, so the block starts at two metres per second.

A4.text: Then energy is kept in the swing. h is v squared over two g. Four over twenty. Zero point two metres.
